title: Introduction to Biochemistry and Cell Biology: Compartments Create Control

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: In a membrane-walled compartment, what sets how much of a molecule that cannot cross the membrane on its own accumulates?
cards.back: A balance: delivery in, against breakdown and export out. When delivery outruns the room's capacity to clear it, the molecule piles up.
cards.quote: So how much of a trapped molecule a room holds is a balance: delivery in, against breakdown and export out.

cards.front: Loss of the lysosomal enzyme hexosaminidase A (HexA) causes {{c1::Tay-Sachs}} disease.
cards.quote: The enzyme is hexosaminidase A (HexA), and the disease is Tay-Sachs.

cards.front: Which three elements make up about 98% of the atoms in an organism?
cards.back: Hydrogen, oxygen and carbon.
cards.quote: Strip an organism down to its atoms and 98% of them are hydrogen, oxygen and carbon.
cards.section: What a cell is made of

cards.front: Carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur, nearly the entire chemical alphabet of biology, are abbreviated {{c1::CHNOPS}}.
cards.quote: Add nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur and you have nearly the entire chemical alphabet of biology: CHNOPS.
cards.section: What a cell is made of

cards.front: Why are O–H and C=O bonds polar?
cards.back: Oxygen is highly electronegative: it pulls the shared electrons toward itself, so the oxygen end is slightly negative and the other end slightly positive.
cards.quote: Oxygen pulls shared electrons strongly toward itself (it is highly electronegative), so in O–H and C=O bonds the electrons sit closer to the oxygen
cards.section: What a cell is made of

cards.front: Why is carbon at the center of biological chemistry?
cards.back: Its four stable bonds build chains, branches and rings, and its chemistry works in water, the medium every cell runs in.
cards.quote: Carbon is at the center because its four stable bonds build chains, branches and rings whose chemistry works in water
cards.section: What a cell is made of

cards.front: Name the four classes of biomolecules and the main job of each.
cards.back: Proteins: workers (enzymes, signals such as insulin). Nucleic acids: the library of information. Carbohydrates: fuel and surface ID tags. Lipids: walls (fats are also dense stored fuel).
cards.quote: Proteins are the workers: enzymes that catalyze reactions, signals like insulin that carry messages.
cards.section: What a cell is made of

cards.front: DNA is written in A, C, G and T; RNA uses A, C, G and {{c1::U}}.
cards.quote: RNA makes the working copies that leave the shelf (A, C, G, U)
cards.section: What a cell is made of

cards.front: How does the structure of a typical membrane lipid make a bilayer form in water?
cards.back: Each lipid has a water-loving head and two water-fearing tails, so in water they line up tail to tail in a double layer with an oily core.
cards.quote: In water they line up tail to tail in a double layer, a bilayer, with an oily core.
cards.section: What a cell is made of

cards.front: A bare lipid bilayer, with no channels or carriers, separates two solutions containing CO₂, glucose and Cl⁻. Which crosses on its own, and why?
cards.back: Only CO₂. Small nonpolar molecules pass straight through the oily core; glucose (polar) and Cl⁻ (charged) need a channel or carrier the cell builds.
cards.quote: Small nonpolar molecules such as O₂ and CO₂ pass straight through the oily core (water crosses too, more slowly).
cards.section: A wall makes a room

cards.front: Why does a ganglioside stay in the membrane layer where it was put?
cards.back: Its big sugar head cannot pass the oily core of the bilayer, so it flips only extremely slowly.
cards.quote: The ganglioside's big sugar head cannot pass the oily core, so it stays in the layer it was put in
cards.section: A wall makes a room

cards.front: The inside of a lysosome sits near pH {{c1::4.5 to 5}}, against about 7.2 in the cytosol.
cards.quote: The inside of a lysosome, the cell's digestive room, sits near pH 4.5 to 5, against about 7.2 in the cytosol
cards.section: A wall makes a room

cards.front: A lysosome is at pH 4.7 and the surrounding cytosol at pH 7.2. About how many times higher is the free H⁺ concentration inside the lysosome?
cards.back: Difference = 7.2 − 4.7 = 2.5 pH units. Each unit is a tenfold step, so 10^2.5 ≈ 316: about 300 times.
cards.quote: Each pH unit is a tenfold step, so the lysosome holds a few hundred times the free H⁺ concentration of the cytosol
cards.section: A wall makes a room

cards.front: What makes DNA replication semi-conservative?
cards.back: DNA polymerase reads one strand and builds its partner, so each new double helix keeps one original strand.
cards.quote: DNA polymerase reads one strand and builds its partner, and the copy is semi-conservative: each new double helix keeps one original strand.
cards.section: The first room: the nucleus and the central dogma

cards.front: In translation, what is a codon, and which molecule matches each codon to its amino acid?
cards.back: A codon is three bases of mRNA; transfer RNA (tRNA) is the matchmaker between code and amino acid, at the ribosome.
cards.quote: Translation reads the mRNA and builds the protein, codon by codon (a codon is three bases), at the ribosome
cards.section: The first room: the nucleus and the central dogma

cards.front: What structural difference suits DNA to long-term storage and RNA to short-lived messages?
cards.back: RNA's ribose carries a 2′-OH, which lets its backbone break much more easily. DNA's deoxyribose has only an H at 2′, so its backbone is far more stable.
cards.quote: RNA's ribose carries an –OH on carbon 2′, which lets its backbone break much more easily, fitting a message the cell uses and discards.
cards.section: The first room: the nucleus and the central dogma

cards.front: Liver cells and neurons carry the same genome. What makes much of the difference between them?
cards.back: Which genes each cell transcribes; a cell does not run every gene at once.
cards.quote: which genes it transcribes is a large part of what makes a liver cell a liver cell and a neuron a neuron
cards.section: The first room: the nucleus and the central dogma

cards.front: Why can bacterial ribosomes start reading an mRNA while it is still being made, when this does not happen for eukaryotic nuclear genes?
cards.back: Bacteria have no nuclear wall, so transcription and translation share one space. In eukaryotes the mRNA is made in the nucleus, spliced and checked, and only then exported through nuclear pores to the cytoplasm.
cards.quote: In bacteria, which have no such wall, ribosomes start reading an mRNA while it is still being made.
cards.section: The first room: the nucleus and the central dogma

cards.front: Suppose a eukaryotic cell lacked its nuclear envelope, so ribosomes could reach each nuclear mRNA as soon as it was made. Predict the effect on control of gene expression.
cards.back: Ribosomes could read messages before they were spliced and checked, so the cell would lose that step of control. Rule: the wall lets the message be spliced and checked before export, one reason eukaryotes regulate genes in ways bacteria cannot.
cards.quote: In your cells the message can be spliced (cut and rejoined) and checked in the nucleus first, and only then exported through the pores in the nuclear membrane.
cards.section: The first room: the nucleus and the central dogma

cards.front: Where are mitochondrial genes transcribed and translated?
cards.back: Inside the mitochondrion, which keeps a small genome of its own.
cards.quote: Mitochondria keep a small genome of their own and transcribe and translate it inside the organelle.
cards.section: The first room: the nucleus and the central dogma

cards.front: How does the internal organization of a prokaryote differ from that of a eukaryote?
cards.back: Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) have few or no internal membranes and no true nucleus; eukaryotes are divided into membrane-enclosed organelles.
cards.quote: Prokaryotes, the bacteria and archaea, are an open floor plan: few or no internal membranes and no true nucleus.
cards.section: Why big cells need inner walls

cards.front: A spherical cell's radius grows from 2 µm to 6 µm. By what factor do its volume and surface area rise, and how many times as much cytoplasm must each square micrometre of membrane now serve?
cards.back: Radius ×3. Volume scales with the cube: 3³ = 27. Surface scales with the square: 3² = 9. Each unit of membrane serves 27 ÷ 9 = 3 times as much cytoplasm.
cards.quote: A cell's volume (the demand for fuel and the waste to clear) rises with the cube of its radius, while its surface
cards.section: Why big cells need inner walls

cards.front: Why does a 10 µm eukaryotic cell make most of its ATP on mitochondrial inner membranes rather than relying on its plasma membrane the way a 1 µm bacterium does for much of its ATP?
cards.back: At ten times the radius, volume grows 1000-fold but surface only 100-fold, so each µm² of outer membrane must serve ten times as much cytoplasm. Of the three options (stay small, stretch thin, fold membrane inside), it folds membrane inside: the mitochondrial inner membrane.
cards.quote: a large cell makes most of its ATP on the folded inner membrane of its mitochondria
cards.section: Why big cells need inner walls

cards.front: A gut absorptive cell loses its microvilli but keeps its internal membranes. Predict the effect on uptake from the gut, and why the internal membranes cannot make up for it.
cards.back: Uptake falls. Uptake from outside depends on plasma membrane area, which microvilli enlarge; internal membranes add area only for jobs done inside the cell.
cards.quote: Uptake from outside still depends on the plasma membrane, which is why absorbing cells such as gut cells fold their outer surface into fine projections (microvilli).
cards.section: Why big cells need inner walls

cards.front: What are the jobs of the rough ER and the smooth ER?
cards.back: Rough ER (ribosomes on its surface) makes proteins to be secreted or sent to membranes and lysosomes. Smooth ER (no ribosomes) makes lipids and detoxifies drugs.
cards.quote: The smooth ER, with no ribosomes, makes lipids and detoxifies drugs (your liver leans on it hard).
cards.section: Why big cells need inner walls

cards.front: In Palade's experiment on guinea pig pancreatic cells, why was a brief pulse of radioactive amino acids followed by a chase with unlabeled ones?
cards.back: So that a single cohort of newly made protein carried the label, and its position could be tracked compartment by compartment over time.
cards.quote: They fed the cells a brief pulse of radioactive amino acids, then chased them with ordinary ones, so a single cohort of new protein carried the label.
cards.section: The sealed conveyor belt, and how we know

cards.front: In a pulse-chase of pancreatic cells, label peaks first over the rough ER, then the Golgi, then secretory granules. What does this show, and what further observation showed the protein is exported?
cards.back: Secreted proteins travel rough ER → Golgi → granules in order. When the cells were stimulated, the granules released their contents and the label appeared outside the cell.
cards.quote: When the cells were stimulated, the granules released their contents and the label appeared outside the cell.
cards.section: The sealed conveyor belt, and how we know

cards.front: In the secretory pathway, misfolded proteins are destroyed by cytosolic machinery, yet properly folded secreted proteins never are. Why?
cards.back: Folded cargo travels a belt of sealed rooms (ER, Golgi, membrane) and never passes through the cytosol. Misfolded proteins that cannot be fixed are pushed back out to the cytosol, where they meet the destroying machinery.
cards.quote: properly folded cargo never meets that protein-destroying machinery
cards.section: The sealed conveyor belt, and how we know

cards.front: Distinguish exocytosis from endocytosis, with one example of each.
cards.back: Exocytosis: a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and releases its cargo outside (insulin from pancreatic beta cells). Endocytosis: the membrane folds inward to bring cargo in (cholesterol via the LDL receptor).
cards.quote: In exocytosis, a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and dumps its cargo outside; this is how a pancreatic beta cell releases insulin into your blood.
cards.section: The sealed conveyor belt, and how we know

cards.front: A cell's LDL receptor is defective. Which uptake route fails, and where does the LDL-cholesterol remain?
cards.back: Endocytosis of cholesterol through the LDL receptor fails, so the cell does not pull it in and it stays in the blood.
cards.quote: In endocytosis, the membrane folds inward to bring cargo in; this is how a cell pulls in cholesterol through its LDL receptor.
cards.section: The sealed conveyor belt, and how we know

cards.front: What two locks protect the cell from the digestive enzymes inside lysosomes?
cards.back: The membrane: the enzymes cannot get out, and targets enter only by routes the cell builds. The acid: the hydrolases work best at acid pH and poorly at the cytosol's.
cards.quote: Lysosomes hold digestive enzymes (hydrolases, which split molecules using water) that would be dangerous loose in the cell, so they sit behind two locks.
cards.section: The recycling room

cards.front: A drug raises the pH inside lysosomes to that of the cytosol without damaging their membranes. Predict the effect on lysosomal digestion.
cards.back: Digestion slows. Lysosomal hydrolases work best at acid pH and poorly at the cytosol's, so they become much less active.
cards.quote: lysosomal hydrolases work best at acid pH and poorly at the cytosol's, so an enzyme that escapes into the cytosol is much less active there
cards.section: The recycling room

cards.front: An acid hydrolase in a fresh liver-cell fraction shows little activity until detergent, which dissolves membranes, is added. What is this hidden activity called, and what does it show?
cards.back: Latency. The test-tube substrate could not cross the membranes until they were dissolved, so the enzymes sit inside sealed membrane bags: lysosomes.
cards.quote: This hidden activity, called latency, was evidence that the enzymes sit inside sealed membrane bags: lysosomes.
cards.section: The recycling room

cards.front: By what two routes does material reach the lysosome?
cards.back: Endocytosis (outside cargo and old patches of plasma membrane) and autophagy (worn-out parts of the cell's interior).
cards.quote: Endocytosis brings in cargo and old patches of plasma membrane; autophagy wraps up worn-out parts of the cell's interior.
cards.section: The recycling room

cards.front: Without HexA, why does GM2 ganglioside stay trapped in the lysosome instead of leaving or being broken down another way?
cards.back: GM2's large, charged sugar head cannot flip through the lysosomal membrane, no transporter carries it out, and no other enzyme can do HexA's job well enough.
cards.quote: GM2's large, charged sugar head cannot flip through the lysosome's membrane, and no transporter carries it out.
cards.section: When one room lacks one enzyme

cards.front: Carriers of Tay-Sachs make about half the normal HexA. Why is the disease recessive?
cards.back: A normal lysosome clears GM2 many times faster than it arrives, so half still keeps up. Storage starts only when clearance falls below delivery, far below half.
cards.why: Like a drain much wider than the tap: halve it and the water sits a little higher but never overflows.
cards.quote: That cut-off is far below half the normal amount, which is why Tay-Sachs is recessive
cards.section: When one room lacks one enzyme

cards.front: A patient's HEXA mutations leave some enzyme activity, but below the cut-off where clearance keeps up with delivery. Compared with the infantile form, predict onset and course.
cards.back: Later onset and slower progression: the leftover enzyme makes the balance tip more slowly, as in the juvenile and adult-onset forms.
cards.quote: In the rarer juvenile and adult-onset forms some enzyme activity remains, so the balance tips more slowly
cards.section: When one room lacks one enzyme

cards.front: In infantile Tay-Sachs every cell carries the broken gene. Give two reasons, from delivery and clearance, that neurons store the most GM2.
cards.back: Delivery is high, because neuron membranes are especially rich in gangliosides. And neurons do not divide, so they keep all they store for life, while a dividing cell splits its load between daughters.
cards.quote: And neurons do not divide: a dividing cell splits its stored GM2 between two daughters at every division
cards.section: When one room lacks one enzyme

cards.front: In infantile Tay-Sachs, do the lysosomes of neurons burst?
cards.back: No. They swell with layered membrane but stay intact; nothing leaks out, and the room fills with something it cannot empty.
cards.quote: The membrane does not burst and nothing leaks out; the room is intact, filling with something it cannot empty.
cards.section: When one room lacks one enzyme

cards.front: A hypothetical enzyme deficiency leaves its unconverted substrate in the blood, and the substrate comes mostly from food. Predict whether diet could treat it, and contrast with GM2 in Tay-Sachs.
cards.back: Diet likely could, as in PKU: the molecule is in the blood and comes from food. GM2 is made in neurons and sealed in their lysosomes behind the blood–brain barrier, so no diet or infused enzyme reaches it.
cards.why: Rule: where the unbroken molecule ends up decides what treatment can reach it.
cards.quote: The difference is where the unbroken molecule ends up.
cards.section: When one room lacks one enzyme

cards.front: What mostly sets how long a given RNA lasts in the cell?
cards.back: Mostly enzymes that destroy it on purpose, not just its fragile 2′-OH backbone; some RNAs, such as those in ribosomes, last a long time.
cards.quote: how long a given RNA lasts in the cell is set mostly by enzymes that destroy it on purpose
cards.section: RNA lifetimes and detours from the dogma

cards.front: Trace the HexA enzyme from its gene to its working site, naming the compartment for each step.
cards.back: HEXA is transcribed in the nucleus; the mRNA is spliced, checked and exported through nuclear pores; it is translated at the rough ER; the Golgi modifies and addresses the protein; it works in the lysosome.
cards.why: Combines the nucleus as the first room with the rough ER making proteins sent to lysosomes and the Golgi addressing them.
cards.quote: The rough ER, ribosomes clinging to its surface, makes proteins that will be secreted or sent to membranes and lysosomes.
cards.section: Why big cells need inner walls

cards.front: Give one bond-chemistry reason and one water-based reason why carbon, not silicon, forms life's backbone.
cards.back: Bonds: C–C bonds are stronger than Si–Si, carbon forms stable double bonds, and silicon chains are attacked by water and oxygen. Water: CO₂ is a soluble gas; SiO₂ is insoluble quartz.
cards.quote: carbon dioxide is a soluble gas that moves freely through blood and air; silicon dioxide is quartz, an insoluble rock
cards.section: Why carbon, not silicon

cards.front: What does reverse transcriptase do, and does Crick's own statement of the central dogma forbid it?
cards.back: It copies RNA into DNA, as in retroviruses such as HIV. Crick's statement allowed it; it forbids information flowing out of protein back into nucleic acid or protein.
cards.quote: Crick's own statement of the central dogma allowed these transfers; what it forbids is information flowing out of protein back into nucleic acid or protein.
cards.section: RNA lifetimes and detours from the dogma

cards.front: An antiviral drug blocks reverse transcriptase. Which step of HIV's life cycle does it stop?
cards.back: Copying the viral RNA into DNA; reverse transcriptase is the enzyme that copies RNA into DNA.
cards.quote: Reverse transcriptase is exactly what some antiviral drugs are built to block.
cards.section: RNA lifetimes and detours from the dogma

cards.front: In a toy lysosome model, GM2 arrives at one tenth of what normal HexA clears at full speed. Why does GM2 never settle once HexA falls to 0.1 of normal or less?
cards.back: At 0.1 the remaining enzyme's full-speed clearance only equals delivery, and below it clearance is lower still, so clearance cannot outrun arrival and GM2 keeps rising.
cards.why: Rule: a trapped molecule settles only where clearance matches delivery.
cards.quote: GM2 arrives at a steady rate, a tenth of what normal HexA can clear at full speed
cards.section: The balance in numbers

cards.front: In the toy lysosome model, a cell with no HexA divides regularly. Predict GM2 per cell over time, and why a neuron does not share this outcome.
cards.back: GM2 per cell levels off, because each division splits the load between daughters. A neuron does not divide, so it gets no such relief and keeps rising.
cards.quote: add cell division and GM2 per cell levels off even with no enzyme, because each division splits the load
cards.section: The balance in numbers

cards.front: Why does losing the GM2 activator protein (the AB variant) block the same step as losing HexA?
cards.back: In the lysosome GM2 sits in small internal membranes; the activator lifts the lipid out so HexA can cut it. Without it, HexA cannot reach GM2.
cards.quote: a helper, the GM2 activator protein, lifts the lipid out so HexA can cut it
cards.section: Partners of HexA

cards.front: In Sandhoff disease the HEXB gene is broken. Which enzymes are lost, and can HexS cover the GM2 cut?
cards.back: Both HexA and HexB are lost, so the GM2 cut fails. HexS can cut GM2, but far too weakly to cover the loss of HexA.
cards.quote: In Sandhoff disease the broken gene is HEXB, which loses both HexA and a related enzyme, HexB.
cards.section: Partners of HexA
